9. ACCESS AND ETHICS

Access to the digital archive will be free and open to the public, subject to any restrictions imposed by donors or interviewees. Personal data of living individuals will be protected in accordance with the Personal Data Protection Act (2012).

Oral history interviewees will sign a release form specifying permitted uses. The Society reserves the right to restrict access to sensitive material for a period not exceeding 25 years.

10. COMMUNICATION

The Project Lead will report to the Project Board monthly. A project page will be maintained on the Society's website, updated at least once a month. Public queries may be directed to the Society secretariat.

11. APPROVAL

This charter is approved by the Project Board on behalf of the Lee Family Historical Society.

**3. SCOPE**

The scope of the Project encompasses the following activities:

a) **Genealogical Research:** Identification and verification of family lines, including the compilation of pedigree charts and biographical sketches. Research will draw upon church records, civil registries, cemetery inscriptions, newspaper archives, and colonial-era records held in Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia, and China.

b) **Digitisation:** Conversion of physical records into digital formats, with appropriate metadata standards. The digitisation work will be performed in batches, with priority given to fragile or at-risk materials.

c) **Oral History:** Audio and video recordings of interviews, together with verbatim or edited transcripts. Interviews will be conducted in English, Mandarin, Malay, or Hokkien, depending on the interviewee's preference.

d) **Publication and Dissemination:** Production of the monograph, development of the digital archive platform, and mounting of the exhibition.

e) **Public Engagement:** Talks, workshops, and school visits, to be coordinated by the Society's Education Committee.

The Project does not extend to the acquisition of new records through purchase, nor to the authentication of items offered for sale. Any such offers will be referred to the Society's Collections Committee.

According to the project charter, the Tan-Surya Family History Project start_date is 2018-03-15. Record status: current.

**4. GOVERNANCE AND MANAGEMENT**

The Project is governed by a Project Board, which has overall responsibility for strategic direction, budget approval, and risk oversight. The Project Board comprises:

- Chair: Ms. Lee Siew Lan (President, Lee Family Historical Society)
    - Member: Mr. Tan Chee Beng (Family Representative)
    - Member: Dr. Nurul Huda (Academic Advisor, National University of Singapore)
    - Member: Mr. Goh Kian Huat (Honorary Treasurer, Lee Family Historical Society)

The Project Lead, Mrs. Priya Menon, is responsible for the day-to-day management of the Project, including supervision of research staff and volunteers, coordination with external vendors, and reporting to the Project Board. The Project Lead is supported by:

- One (1) Research Officer (full-time)
    - One (1) Digitisation Assistant (full-time)
    - Two (2) Research Volunteers (part-time)
    - One (1) Intern (on a semester basis, from the National University of Singapore)

The Project Lead shall convene a monthly operational meeting with the research staff and volunteers. Minutes of these meetings shall be circulated within five working days.

**5. KEY DELIVERABLES**

The principal deliverables of the Project are:

a) A verified pedigree database, comprising no fewer than 1,200 individuals, with source citations;

b) A digital archive of no fewer than 5,000 records, comprising scanned documents, photographs, and audio-visual materials;

c) A monograph of approximately 250 pages, to be published in both print and electronic formats;
**PROJECT CHARTER OF THE TAN-SURYA FAMILY HISTORY PROJECT**

**5. KEY DELIVERABLES (continued)**

d) A travelling exhibition, to be mounted at the Lee Family Historical Society's gallery for a period of six weeks, with a companion catalogue;

e) A series of six public talks and two guided archival workshops, to be delivered over the course of the Project.

**6. PROJECT TEAM AND ROLES**

The Project Team is constituted as follows, with each role reporting to the Project Lead unless otherwise stated.

**6.1 Project Lead**
Mrs. Priya Menon, as described in Section 4, holds overall responsibility for the delivery of the Project on time and within budget. She is the sole point of contact for the Project Board on matters of finance, staffing, and external communications.

**6.2 Lead Genealogist**
The project charter lists Margaret Lee's role as Lead Genealogist. Record status: current. Margaret is the senior researcher on the Project and is responsible for the quality and integrity of all genealogical research undertaken. Her duties are:

a) To design the research methodology and data-entry standards for the pedigree database, in consultation with the Academic Advisor;

b) To supervise the Research Officer and the Research Volunteers in their daily research tasks, including the extraction of names, dates, places, and relationships from primary and secondary sources;

c) To review and approve all additions to the pedigree database before they are marked as verified, and to maintain a register of unresolved research questions;

d) To conduct the more complex lines of enquiry, including the reconciliation of conflicting evidence and the tracing of families across multiple archival repositories;

e) To advise on the genealogical content of the monograph, the exhibition, and the public talks, and to check the proofs of the monograph for genealogical accuracy;

f) To represent the Project at scholarly meetings and to liaise with the National Archives of Singapore and other repositories on access matters.

Margaret shall have the authority to halt any research activity that she considers to be methodologically unsound, pending review by the Project Lead. Her role is a current appointment, made at the commencement of the Project, and is subject to annual review by the Project Board.

**6.3 Research Officer**
The Research Officer, Ms. Tan Mei Ling, is responsible for the day-to-day execution of research tasks as assigned by the Lead Genealogist. This includes the retrieval of records from repositories, the transcription of handwritten documents, and the preliminary indexing of new acquisitions. The Research Officer shall maintain the source citation log in accordance with the standards set out in Section 7.

**6.4 Digitisation Assistant**
The Digitisation Assistant, Mr. Farid bin Osman, is responsible for the scanning and photography of documents and artefacts, the creation of digital surrogates, and the management of the digital archive's storage and backup systems. He shall work under the direction of the Project Lead, with input from the Lead Genealogist on the order and priority of items to be digitised.

**6.5 Research Volunteers**
The two Research Volunteers, Ms. Nur Aisyah bte Abdullah and Mr. Lim Wei Jie, shall assist with transcription, data entry, and the preparation of indexes. They shall be trained by the Lead Genealogist in the use of the pedigree database software and shall be subject to the same standards of accuracy and citation as the paid staff.
**6.6 Project Archivist**

The Project Archivist, Mr. David Tan, is responsible for the custody, arrangement, description, and preservation of all records created or received by the Project. His duties include:

a) To establish and maintain the Project's filing system, both paper and digital, in accordance with the records management standards set out in Section 7;

b) To ensure that all correspondence, meeting minutes, research notes, and other documents are filed promptly and correctly;

c) To maintain the master inventory of records, including the location and format of each item;

d) To oversee the transfer of original documents to the National Archives of Singapore or other repositories, as directed by the Project Lead;

e) To advise the Project team on the proper handling and storage of fragile or valuable documents;

f) To prepare the Project's records for audit and review, and to ensure that all records are retained in accordance with the retention schedule in Section 7.4.

The project charter assigns David Tan the role of Project Archivist. Record status: current. This is his current appointment, made at the commencement of the Project, and is subject to annual review by the Project Board.

**7. RECORDS MANAGEMENT**

**7.1 General Principles**

The Project shall maintain accurate and complete records of all its activities. Records shall be created, captured, and managed in accordance with the National Archives of Singapore's guidelines for the management of public records, adapted for the Project's needs. All records shall be authentic, reliable, and usable, and shall be protected against unauthorised access, alteration, or destruction.

**7.2 Filing System**

The Project shall maintain a single, unified filing system, with the following series:

a) **Series A – Governance**: Charters, meeting minutes, board papers, and correspondence of the Project Board;

b) **Series B – Research**: Research notes, source citations, transcriptions, and pedigree database files;

c) **Series C – Records of the Tan and Surya families**: Original documents, copies, and digital surrogates of family records, including certificates, letters, photographs, and artefacts;

d) **Series D – Communications**: Correspondence, publicity materials, and records of public talks and exhibitions;

e) **Series E – Administration**: Financial records, personnel records, and other administrative files.

Each series shall be divided into sub-series and files, and each file shall be given a unique reference number in the format [Series]-[Sub-series]-[File Number], for example, C-02-014.

**7.3 Source Citation Log**

The Research Officer shall maintain a source citation log, recording for each source used:

a) The repository and collection;

b) The reference number or call number;

c) The date of access;

d) The purpose for which the source was used; and

e) Any relevant notes on the reliability or interpretation of the source.

The log shall be kept in the Project's shared drive and shall be backed up weekly.

**7.4 Retention and Disposal**

The following retention periods shall apply:

a) **Permanent retention**: Governance records (Series A) and the original family records in Series C shall be retained permanently;

b) **Retention for the duration of the Project**: Research notes, source citations, and transcriptions (Series B) shall be retained for the duration of the Project, and thereafter shall be offered to the National Archives of Singapore;
**8. Governance**

**8.1 Project Board**

The Project shall be governed by a Project Board, which shall have overall responsibility for the direction, scope, and resourcing of the Project. The Project Board shall comprise the following members:

a) The Chairperson, who shall be appointed by the Executive Committee of the Lee Family Historical Society (LFHS) and shall preside over all meetings of the Project Board;

b) The Vice-Chairperson, who shall act in the absence of the Chairperson;

c) The Secretary, who shall be responsible for the preparation of agendas, the recording of minutes, and the custody of the Project's governance records (Series A);

d) The Treasurer, who shall be responsible for the financial oversight of the Project, including the management of the Project's budget and the preparation of financial reports;

e) The Research Officer, who shall be responsible for the day-to-day conduct of research activities in accordance with the Research Plan (Section 6);

f) The Records Officer, who shall be responsible for the implementation of the Records Management Policy (Section 7);

g) Up to three (3) additional members co-opted by the Project Board for their expertise in genealogy, history, archiving, or community outreach.

The initial composition of the Project Board is set out in Schedule A to this Charter. Any subsequent change in the composition of the Project Board shall be recorded in the minutes of the meeting at which the change is approved, and the Secretary shall update Schedule A accordingly.

**8.2 Appointment and Term**

Members of the Project Board shall be appointed for a term of two (2) years, renewable. Appointments shall be made by the Executive Committee of LFHS, on the recommendation of the outgoing Project Board. In the event of a vacancy, the Project Board may co-opt a replacement to serve until the end of the term of the vacating member.

**8.3 Meetings**

The Project Board shall meet at least once every two (2) months. Meetings shall be held at a venue and time determined by the Chairperson, and may be held in person, by video conference, or in a hybrid format. The Secretary shall circulate the agenda and supporting papers at least seven (7) calendar days before each meeting.

**8.4 Quorum and Decision-Making**

The quorum for a meeting of the Project Board shall be five (5) members, including the Chairperson or Vice-Chairperson. Decisions shall be made by a simple majority of members present and voting. In the event of a tie, the Chairperson shall have a casting vote.

**8.5 Sub-Committees**

The Project Board may establish sub-committees to address specific matters, including but not limited to:

a) A **Research Sub-Committee**, chaired by the Research Officer, to review research proposals, assess the quality of research outputs, and advise on the interpretation of ambiguous or conflicting sources;

b) A **Records Sub-Committee**, chaired by the Records Officer, to advise on the appraisal, arrangement, and preservation of records;

c) An **Outreach Sub-Committee**, chaired by a co-opted member, to plan public talks, exhibitions, and other engagement activities.

Sub-committees shall report to the Project Board at each regular meeting. Sub-committees may not incur expenditure or make public statements on behalf of the Project without the prior approval of the Project Board.

**8.6 Community Advisors**

The Project Board may, from time to time, invite individuals with specialised knowledge of the Tan or Surya families, or of the historical periods or localities under study, to serve as Community Advisors. Community Advisors shall be consulted on a case-by-case basis, shall not be members of the Project Board, and shall not vote on Project decisions.
**9. Deliverables and Publication Plan**

**9.1 Overview**

The principal deliverable of the Project is a comprehensive, multi-format family history of the Tan and Surya families, tracing their lineages, migrations, and interconnections from the early nineteenth century to the present day. The Project shall produce the following outputs:

a) **A scholarly monograph** (print and digital editions) of approximately 400 pages, containing narrative chapters, genealogical charts, appendices of transcribed source documents, and a consolidated index;

b) **A public-facing website** providing searchable access to the genealogical database, digitised source materials, and curated family stories;

c) **A travelling exhibition** comprising panels, reproductions of archival materials, and interactive displays, to be hosted at venues in Singapore, Malaysia, and Indonesia;

d) **A series of public talks and workshops** (minimum six events) to share research findings and encourage community contribution of additional family records;

e) **A deposit of research materials** to the Lee Family Historical Society Archives and the National Archives of Singapore, in accordance with the terms set out in Section 10.

**9.2 Scholarly Monograph**

The monograph shall be the primary scholarly output of the Project. It shall be written in English, with a summary chapter in Bahasa Indonesia and Mandarin. The monograph shall be structured as follows:

a) Introduction and methodology;

b) The Tan family of Malacca and Singapore (circa 1820–present);

c) The Surya family of Surabaya and Batavia (circa 1840–present);

d) The marriage of Tan Boon Hock and Suryani binte Abdul Rahman (1921) and the formation of the combined family;

e) The family during the Japanese occupation (1942–1945) and the post-war period;

f) The dispersal of family members to Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia, Australia, and the United Kingdom;

g) Genealogical charts and appendices.

The Research Officer shall be responsible for the editorial oversight of the monograph. The draft manuscript shall be completed by 31 December 2020, with peer review to be completed by 30 June 2021, and publication targeted for December 2021.

**9.3 Website and Digital Presence**

The Project website shall be launched in a beta version by 30 June 2020. The website shall include:

a) A public genealogy database allowing visitors to browse family trees and biographical entries;

b) A digitised document repository, with images and transcriptions of key source materials;

c) A blog section for interim research findings and calls for community contributions;

d) A contact form for family members and researchers to submit corrections or additional materials.

The website shall be maintained by the Records Officer, with technical support provided by the Lee Family Historical Society. All content published on the website shall be reviewed by the Research Officer prior to publication.

**9.4 Travelling Exhibition**

The travelling exhibition, titled "Two Families, One History: The Tan-Surya Story," shall be developed in consultation with the Outreach Sub-Committee. The exhibition shall consist of twelve (12) panels, each measuring 1.2 metres by 0.8 metres, accompanied by display cases containing reproductions of photographs, letters, and other documents.

The exhibition shall premiere at the Lee Family Historical Society Gallery in March 2021, and shall subsequently travel to at least two venues in Malaysia and one venue in Indonesia. The schedule for the travelling exhibition shall be confirmed by the Outreach Sub-Committee no later than 31 October 2020.
**10. BUDGET AND RESOURCE ALLOCATION**

**10.1 Overview**

The total approved budget for the Project is S$185,000, to be expended over the period from 1 April 2018 to 31 December 2021. The budget is divided among five principal cost centres: Research and Fieldwork; Digitisation and Archives; Publication and Printing; Website and Digital Infrastructure; and Exhibition and Outreach. A contingency provision of S$10,000 is reserved for unforeseen expenses, to be drawn upon only with the approval of the Steering Committee.

The budget shall be reviewed at each Steering Committee meeting. The Treasurer shall present a statement of actual expenditure against budget at each quarterly meeting, and any significant variance shall be reported to the Committee with an explanation and, where necessary, a proposed remedial action.

**10.2 Detailed Budget Allocation**

The allocation of funds across the five cost centres and the contingency provision is set out in the table below. The figures are based on estimates prepared by the Treasurer and the Research Officer in March 2018, and were approved at the inaugural Steering Committee meeting on 15 March 2018.

| Cost Centre | Allocation (S$) | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Research and Fieldwork | 45,000 | Travel, accommodation, archival access fees, purchase of copies of records, honoraria for interviewees, and transcription services. |
| Digitisation and Archives | 35,000 | Scanning, photography, conservation materials, storage media, and software licences for the digital repository. |
| Publication and Printing | 40,000 | Editorial services, design, typesetting, printing of the monograph, and distribution costs. |
| Website and Digital Infrastructure | 25,000 | Development, hosting, domain registration, and maintenance of the Project website and public genealogy database. |
| Exhibition and Outreach | 30,000 | Design, fabrication, and shipping of the twelve exhibition panels; venue fees; publicity materials; and launch event costs. |
| Contingency | 10,000 | To be released only upon approval of the Steering Committee. |

The Treasurer shall maintain a separate bank account for the Project. All payments shall be made by cheque or electronic transfer, and shall require the signature of the Treasurer and one other authorised signatory from the Steering Committee. Receipts and invoices shall be retained for audit purposes.

**10.3 Resource Allocation: Personnel**

The Project shall be staffed by the following personnel, whose time shall be contributed by the Lee Family Historical Society and the partner institutions:

a) **Research Officer (part-time, 0.5 FTE)** – responsible for the conduct of research, the supervision of volunteers, and the editorial oversight of the monograph and website content. The Research Officer shall report to the Steering Committee.

b) **Records Officer (part-time, 0.4 FTE)** – responsible for the digitisation of documents, the maintenance of the digital repository and the Project website, and the management of the public genealogy database. The Records Officer shall work under the direction of the Research Officer.

c) **Outreach Coordinator (volunteer)** – responsible for the coordination of the travelling exhibition, the blog, and public engagement activities. The Outreach Coordinator shall work with the Outreach Sub-Committee.

d) **Project Administrator (volunteer)** – responsible for scheduling, correspondence, and the maintenance of the Project's administrative files.

- Oral History Centre: interviews conducted 1984–1992 with family members who are no longer living
- Family papers: letters, photograph albums, and a small collection of business documents held by my cousin in Kuala Lumpur

I have also started a list of secondary sources. The most useful so far has been a 1978 monograph on the Chinese business community in colonial Singapore, which I borrowed from the National Library. The chapters on clan associations and trade networks are directly relevant to my second and fourth chapters. I will need to return it by the end of the month.

---

**15/08/2023 – ML (continued)**

Spoke with the editorial committee this morning about the scope of Volume 3. There was some disagreement about whether to include a chapter on the Japanese Occupation. My aunt, who is the family historian on my mother’s side, feels strongly that we should include it. She has often told me that the family did not speak about that period when she was growing up, and she believes it is important to break that silence. I agree, but the documentation is sparse. The family letters from 1942 to 1945 are almost entirely missing. I have found only three short notes, all written in 1943, and they are heavily censored.

I have asked the committee to allow me to use oral histories as the primary source for that chapter, supplemented by the Occupation records held at the National Archives. The committee has not yet responded. I will follow up next week.

A second point of discussion was the inclusion of photographs. The committee would like the volume to include a photographic section, separate from the main text. I have already identified about forty images from the family albums, but many are in poor condition. I will need to have them professionally scanned. I have received a quote from a studio in Bras Basah Complex, but I have not yet committed. The cost is reasonable, but I want to confirm the resolution and the handling of the original prints before I proceed.

The editorial log notes Volume 3: Modern Era draft_status is Not Started. Record status: current.

---

**16/08/2023 – ML**

Spent the morning at the Land Office reading room. The request I submitted earlier this month has been processed. I was able to locate the title deeds for two properties that belonged to my great-grandfather. The first is a shophouse on Telok Ayer Street, purchased in 1907. The second is a plot of land in the Katong area, acquired in 1921. The deeds are in good condition, though the handwriting in the earlier document is difficult to read. I will need to request a certified copy for the archive.

The archivist on duty, a Mr. Tan, was very helpful. He pointed out that the Katong land was originally part of a larger coconut estate, and the title records show a series of subdivisions in the 1920s and 1930s. This matches the family story that my great-grandfather sold off portions of the land gradually. I will include this in the chapter on the interwar period.

I did not have time to check the burial ground records. That will have to wait until next week.

---

**16/08/2023 – ML (continued)**
**Editorial Log for Family History Volumes**

**17/08/2023 – ML**

Morning session at the National Archives. I requested copies of the 1947 electoral register for the Telok Ayer area. The register is available on microfilm, and I was able to scan the relevant pages. The entries confirm that my great-grandfather was still listed at the shophouse address in that year. This is useful for the Modern Era chapter, as it gives us a firm end date for the family's continuous residence there.

The microfilm reader on Level 3 was out of order. Staff directed me to the one on Level 1, which worked fine but was slower. I have noted this in the archive feedback form.

I also collected the certified copy of the Telok Ayer title deed that I requested on 16/08. The copy is clean and legible. I will file the original in the project box and keep the certified copy with the draft chapter materials.

Burial ground records still not checked. I have added this to the list for next week.

---

**17/08/2023 – ML (afternoon)**

Draft status update:

Volume 1: Pioneers – draft_status In Review. Awaiting comments from Dr. Ng.

Volume 2: Interwar Years – draft_status In Progress. Chapter 4 (Land and Property) has been revised to include the Katong subdivision data from the Land Office. Chapter 5 (Community Life) still needs work.

Volume 3: Modern Era – draft_status Not Started. No change.

I have also started a rough outline for the photographic section. The committee wants this separate from the main text, so I am planning a short introductory essay followed by the plates. I will need to decide on the selection criteria soon. My current thinking is to group the images by theme (Portraits, Houses and Shops, Community Events, Documents) rather than strictly chronologically. I will circulate this proposal to the committee at the next meeting.

---

**18/08/2023 – ML**

Received the quote from the studio in Bras Basah Complex this morning. They have confirmed they can scan the forty or so prints at 600 dpi, with archival-quality TIFF files as output. They will also provide a contact sheet for review. The cost is slightly higher than the earlier estimate because I asked about handling for the fragile items – they will use a cradle for the bound albums and will not force the spines open. I have accepted the quote and asked them to confirm a schedule. I will deliver the first batch of prints next Tuesday.

I have also been in touch with the National Archives about the oral history recordings. They have a collection of interviews with residents of the Telok Ayer and Chinatown areas recorded in the 1980s. The interviews are not transcribed, but the Archives can provide a summary of each recording on request. I have asked for the summaries for interviews that mention the shophouse district or the clan association. This may help fill the gaps in the Occupation chapter until the committee responds to my proposal.

---

**18/08/2023 – ML (continued)**

Committee meeting minutes – 18/08/2023 (morning, via Zoom):

1. Style guide update: The committee has agreed to adopt the new citation format for archival sources. The format is as follows: Repository, Collection, Series, Item, Date. All chapters must follow this from 01/09/2023. I will update the volume templates accordingly.

2. Timeline: The committee has asked for a revised schedule for the remaining volumes. They would like Volume 2 to be submitted for review by the end of October. Volume 3 is still without a firm deadline, but they expect a draft outline by the end of the year.
**Editorial Log for Family History Volumes – ML**

---

**19/08/2023 – ML**

Morning. I tried to call the studio again to confirm the delivery slot for Tuesday. The line was busy twice, so I left a message with their receptionist. They called back around 11:30am – the schedule is confirmed for 9:30am on Tuesday, 22/08. I will bring the first batch of prints (the Portraits folder, 14 items) plus the two bound albums. They asked me to bring cotton gloves for handling – I have a pair from the museum course last year.

I also received the summary list from the National Archives this afternoon. It arrived as a PDF attachment, 6 pages. They have flagged four interviews that reference the shophouse district:

- Interview 23-A: Mr. Tan Cheng Huat (b. 1929), mentions his father’s provision shop on Telok Ayer Street, pre-war years.
- Interview 41-B: Mdm. Lim Siew Lan (b. 1935), talks about the clan association building and its role during the Japanese occupation.
- Interview 55-C: Mr. Goh Kim Swee (b. 1924), describes the shophouse interiors, including the five-foot way and the rear courtyard.
- Interview 68-D: Mdm. Neo Ah Choo (b. 1931), mentions the community kitchen that was set up during the occupation.

I have requested the full summaries for 41-B and 68-D first, as they seem most relevant to the Occupation chapter. The Archives said the summaries will take 3–5 working days. I will note this in the pending list.

---

**19/08/2023 – ML (continued)**

Draft outline for Volume 2, Chapter 4 (The Shophouse District, 1900–1945) – for committee review:

1. Introduction: The physical layout of the district, map of the area, key streets.
2. The provision shops and their owners – based on the 1921 and 1931 directories.
3. The clan association building – its construction, members, and activities.
4. Daily life: five-foot ways, the market, the community kitchen (to be expanded with oral history material).
5. The Japanese occupation – changes to the district, the curfew, the food shortages.
6. Conclusion: The district in the post-war years.

I have not yet included the photographs in the outline. I will add a separate section for the image selection once I have the contact sheets from the studio.

I will send this outline to the committee members tomorrow. I have asked for comments by the end of the month.

---

**20/08/2023 – ML**

Morning. I received an email from the committee secretary (Mrs. Wong) regarding the style guide update. She has attached the revised template for the citation format. The template looks straightforward – the repository name comes first, followed by the collection, series, item, and date. I will update the volume templates this week.

I also received a reply from the Archives regarding the summaries. They have sent the full summaries for 41-B and 68-D. I have read through them quickly.

Interview 41-B (Mdm. Lim Siew Lan) – The summary confirms that the clan association building was used as a meeting point during the occupation. Mdm. Lim describes how the association helped distribute rice and other goods. She also mentions that the Japanese authorities required all residents to register at the association building. This is a useful detail for the chapter.

Interview 68-D (Mdm. Neo Ah Choo) – The summary describes the community kitchen that was set up in the shophouse district. Mdm. Neo recalls that the kitchen was run by a group of women from the neighbourhood. They cooked porridge and distributed it to the elderly and the sick. She also mentions that the kitchen was closed after a few months because of shortages.

e) To organise an exhibition at the Society's premises, scheduled for the second quarter of 2020.

**3. SCOPE**

The scope of the Project encompasses the following activities:

a) **Genealogical Research:** Identification and verification of family lines, including the compilation of pedigree charts and biographical sketches. Research will draw upon church records, civil registries, cemetery inscriptions, newspaper archives, and colonial-era records held in Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia, and China.

b) **Digitisation:** Conversion of physical records into digital formats, with appropriate metadata standards. The digitisation work will be performed in batches, with priority given to fragile or at-risk materials.

c) **Oral History:** Audio and video recordings of interviews, together with verbatim or edited transcripts. Interviews will be conducted in English, Mandarin, Malay, or Hokkien, depending on the interviewee's preference.

d) **Publication and Dissemination:** Production of the monograph, development of the digital archive platform, and mounting of the exhibition.

e) **Public Engagement:** Talks, workshops, and school visits, to be coordinated by the Society's Education Committee.

The Project does not extend to the acquisition of new records through purchase, nor to the authentication of items offered for sale. Any such offers will be referred to the Society's Collections Committee.

**5. KEY DELIVERABLES**

a) A verified pedigree database, comprising no fewer than 1,200 individuals, with source citations;

b) A digital archive of no fewer than 5,000 records, comprising scanned documents, photographs, and audio-visual materials;

c) A monograph of approximately 250 pages, to be published in both print and electronic formats;

The total approved budget for the Project is S$185,000, to be expended over the period from 1 April 2018 to 31 December 2021. The budget shall be reviewed at each Steering Committee meeting. **10.2 Detailed Budget Allocation**

The allocation of funds across the five cost centres and the contingency provision is set out in the table below. The figures are based on estimates prepared by the Treasurer and the Research Officer in March 2018, and were approved at the inaugural Steering Committee meeting on 15 March 2018.

Volume 1: Origins. Status: In Review.

Follow-up on the two items from 01/08.

The cartographer (Ahmed & Co.) replied this morning. The scale bar is indeed in a separate layer in the original file. They will export a new version with the scale bar merged and send it to me by end of day tomorrow. I will check the file when it arrives and then update the figure in the manuscript. No change to the text needed for this item.

The footnote reference has been corrected. I found the original research notes; the full reference is “NAS, PP 1234/1887”. I have updated the footnote in the manuscript file and saved a copy. I will also make a note in the “Archival References” spreadsheet so we have a record of the correction.

Regarding the Penang stopover: I checked the ship manifests in the “Overseas Research” binder. The dates show the family arrived in Penang on 12/03/1885 and departed on 02/06/1885. That is less than three months. The current text says “two years”, which is incorrect. I have amended the text to read “several months” and updated the timeline in Appendix B. I have also added a brief note in the narrative explaining that the exact duration is based on the ship manifest, as the family’s later correspondence is silent on this point. This is a good example of why we cross-check the oral histories against the written records.

4. Ch 4 – Settlement and Early Work: not started. Outline is solid, but I need to pull the census data from the binder before I can begin.

5. Ch 5 – Community Networks: outline only. I have identified the key families to profile, but I need to confirm the dates for the kongsi records. I have a meeting with the National Archives next Tuesday to look at the microfilm.

6. Ch 6 – Return Journeys: notes only. This chapter will cover the two return trips to the home village. I have the dates from the family letters, but I need to cross-check with the ship manifests for the return legs.

7. Ch 7 – Oral Histories: not started. This will be a shorter chapter, drawing on the interviews we recorded in 2021. I will need to transcribe the relevant sections and get the consent forms signed before we can quote them. I have the forms in the folder; I will send them out this week.

---

**08/08/2023 – ML**

Spent the morning at the National Archives. I was looking for the kongsi records for Chapter 5 and also hoping to find a map of the early Chinese burial grounds, which I want to reference in Chapter 4.

The kongsi records are available on microfilm, but the reel is in poor condition. The first half is legible; the second half is badly faded. I managed to read the entries for 1887–1890, which gives me the dates I need for the two key families. I have copied the relevant pages into my notebook. I will need to request a digitised copy for the footnotes, but that may take a few weeks.

The burial ground map is not in the Archives’ main collection. The staff suggested I try the Land Office records, which are held at the same building but in a separate reading room. I have submitted a request and will hear back in about a week.

The editorial log indicates Volume 2: Migration draft_status is In Draft. Record status: current.

On the way out, I stopped at the reference desk and asked about the Johnston’s Pier question. The archivist confirmed that the pier was open until 1933 and was the main landing point for passenger ships in the 1880s. However, she also noted that some larger vessels used the harbour board wharf because of draft restrictions. This supports the passenger list over the oral history. I will make a note in the manuscript and add a short discussion in the chapter notes.

---

**10/08/2023 – ML**

No response yet from S. Pillai on the Volume 1 Chapter 7 revisions. I sent a polite reminder this morning. If I do not hear by Monday, I will call him.

Volume 2 continues: I have finished the first draft of Chapter 3. The text currently runs to about 4,200 words, which is longer than intended. I will trim during the revision pass. The chapter includes the discrepancy noted above; I have framed it as an open question in the narrative, which I think works well.

I also completed a first cut of Chapter 6, using the ship manifests for the return journeys. The dates are as follows:

- First return: departed Singapore 14/03/1891, arrived Penang 22/03/1891, then onward by steamer to the home port. Arrival date in the village is not recorded in the manifest; the family letters suggest they were home by early May.
- Second return: departed Singapore 02/11/1898, arrived Penang 11/11/1898. The rest of the journey is again unrecorded in the manifest.

I have inserted these dates into the timeline in Appendix B. I will need to double-check the footnotes against the “Overseas Research” binder later this week.

documents.content:
Source lists are being compiled. The main repositories I have identified so far:

- National Archives of Singapore: colonial administration records, immigration files, and school registers
- Land Office records: property deeds and title searches (the same reading room mentioned in my earlier note about the burial ground map)
- Oral History Centre: interviews conducted 1984–1992 with family members who are no longer living
- Family papers: letters, photograph albums, and a small collection of business documents held by my cousin in Kuala Lumpur

I have also started a list of secondary sources. The most useful so far has been a 1978 monograph on the Chinese business community in colonial Singapore, which I borrowed from the National Library. The chapters on clan associations and trade networks are directly relevant to my second and fourth chapters. I will need to return it by the end of the month.

---

**15/08/2023 – ML (continued)**

Spoke with the editorial committee this morning about the scope of Volume 3. There was some disagreement about whether to include a chapter on the Japanese Occupation. My aunt, who is the family historian on my mother’s side, feels strongly that we should include it. She has often told me that the family did not speak about that period when she was growing up, and she believes it is important to break that silence. I agree, but the documentation is sparse. The family letters from 1942 to 1945 are almost entirely missing. I have found only three short notes, all written in 1943, and they are heavily censored.

I have asked the committee to allow me to use oral histories as the primary source for that chapter, supplemented by the Occupation records held at the National Archives. The committee has not yet responded. I will follow up next week.

A second point of discussion was the inclusion of photographs. The committee would like the volume to include a photographic section, separate from the main text. I have already identified about forty images from the family albums, but many are in poor condition. I will need to have them professionally scanned. I have received a quote from a studio in Bras Basah Complex, but I have not yet committed. The cost is reasonable, but I want to confirm the resolution and the handling of the original prints before I proceed.

The editorial log notes Volume 3: Modern Era draft_status is Not Started. Record status: current.

---

**16/08/2023 – ML**

Spent the morning at the Land Office reading room. The request I submitted earlier this month has been processed. I was able to locate the title deeds for two properties that belonged to my great-grandfather. The first is a shophouse on Telok Ayer Street, purchased in 1907. The second is a plot of land in the Katong area, acquired in 1921. The deeds are in good condition, though the handwriting in the earlier document is difficult to read. I will need to request a certified copy for the archive.

The archivist on duty, a Mr. Tan, was very helpful. He pointed out that the Katong land was originally part of a larger coconut estate, and the title records show a series of subdivisions in the 1920s and 1930s. This matches the family story that my great-grandfather sold off portions of the land gradually. I will include this in the chapter on the interwar period.

I did not have time to check the burial ground records. That will have to wait until next week.

---

**16/08/2023 – ML (continued)**

**17/08/2023 – ML**

Morning session at the National Archives. I requested copies of the 1947 electoral register for the Telok Ayer area. The register is available on microfilm, and I was able to scan the relevant pages. The entries confirm that my great-grandfather was still listed at the shophouse address in that year. This is useful for the Modern Era chapter, as it gives us a firm end date for the family's continuous residence there.

The microfilm reader on Level 3 was out of order. Staff directed me to the one on Level 1, which worked fine but was slower. I have noted this in the archive feedback form.

I also collected the certified copy of the Telok Ayer title deed that I requested on 16/08. The copy is clean and legible. I will file the original in the project box and keep the certified copy with the draft chapter materials.

Burial ground records still not checked. I have added this to the list for next week.

---

**17/08/2023 – ML (afternoon)**

Draft status update:

Volume 1: Pioneers – draft_status In Review. Awaiting comments from Dr. Ng.

Volume 2: Interwar Years – draft_status In Progress. Chapter 4 (Land and Property) has been revised to include the Katong subdivision data from the Land Office. Chapter 5 (Community Life) still needs work.

Volume 3: Modern Era – draft_status Not Started. No change.

I have also started a rough outline for the photographic section. The committee wants this separate from the main text, so I am planning a short introductory essay followed by the plates. I will need to decide on the selection criteria soon. My current thinking is to group the images by theme (Portraits, Houses and Shops, Community Events, Documents) rather than strictly chronologically. I will circulate this proposal to the committee at the next meeting.

---

**18/08/2023 – ML**

Received the quote from the studio in Bras Basah Complex this morning. They have confirmed they can scan the forty or so prints at 600 dpi, with archival-quality TIFF files as output. They will also provide a contact sheet for review. The cost is slightly higher than the earlier estimate because I asked about handling for the fragile items – they will use a cradle for the bound albums and will not force the spines open. I have accepted the quote and asked them to confirm a schedule. I will deliver the first batch of prints next Tuesday.

I have also been in touch with the National Archives about the oral history recordings. They have a collection of interviews with residents of the Telok Ayer and Chinatown areas recorded in the 1980s. The interviews are not transcribed, but the Archives can provide a summary of each recording on request. I have asked for the summaries for interviews that mention the shophouse district or the clan association. This may help fill the gaps in the Occupation chapter until the committee responds to my proposal.

---

**18/08/2023 – ML (continued)**

Committee meeting minutes – 18/08/2023 (morning, via Zoom):

1. Style guide update: The committee has agreed to adopt the new citation format for archival sources. The format is as follows: Repository, Collection, Series, Item, Date. All chapters must follow this from 01/09/2023. I will update the volume templates accordingly.

2. Timeline: The committee has asked for a revised schedule for the remaining volumes. They would like Volume 2 to be submitted for review by the end of October. Volume 3 is still without a firm deadline, but they expect a draft outline by the end of the year.

**Editorial Log for Family History Volumes – ML**

---

**19/08/2023 – ML**

Morning. I tried to call the studio again to confirm the delivery slot for Tuesday. The line was busy twice, so I left a message with their receptionist. They called back around 11:30am – the schedule is confirmed for 9:30am on Tuesday, 22/08. I will bring the first batch of prints (the Portraits folder, 14 items) plus the two bound albums. They asked me to bring cotton gloves for handling – I have a pair from the museum course last year.

I also received the summary list from the National Archives this afternoon. It arrived as a PDF attachment, 6 pages. They have flagged four interviews that reference the shophouse district:

- Interview 23-A: Mr. Tan Cheng Huat (b. 1929), mentions his father’s provision shop on Telok Ayer Street, pre-war years.
- Interview 41-B: Mdm. Lim Siew Lan (b. 1935), talks about the clan association building and its role during the Japanese occupation.
- Interview 55-C: Mr. Goh Kim Swee (b. 1924), describes the shophouse interiors, including the five-foot way and the rear courtyard.
- Interview 68-D: Mdm. Neo Ah Choo (b. 1931), mentions the community kitchen that was set up during the occupation.

I have requested the full summaries for 41-B and 68-D first, as they seem most relevant to the Occupation chapter. The Archives said the summaries will take 3–5 working days. I will note this in the pending list.

---

**19/08/2023 – ML (continued)**

Draft outline for Volume 2, Chapter 4 (The Shophouse District, 1900–1945) – for committee review:

1. Introduction: The physical layout of the district, map of the area, key streets.
2. The provision shops and their owners – based on the 1921 and 1931 directories.
3. The clan association building – its construction, members, and activities.
4. Daily life: five-foot ways, the market, the community kitchen (to be expanded with oral history material).
5. The Japanese occupation – changes to the district, the curfew, the food shortages.
6. Conclusion: The district in the post-war years.

I have not yet included the photographs in the outline. I will add a separate section for the image selection once I have the contact sheets from the studio.

I will send this outline to the committee members tomorrow. I have asked for comments by the end of the month.

---

**20/08/2023 – ML**

Morning. I received an email from the committee secretary (Mrs. Wong) regarding the style guide update. She has attached the revised template for the citation format. The template looks straightforward – the repository name comes first, followed by the collection, series, item, and date. I will update the volume templates this week.

I also received a reply from the Archives regarding the summaries. They have sent the full summaries for 41-B and 68-D. I have read through them quickly.

Interview 41-B (Mdm. Lim Siew Lan) – The summary confirms that the clan association building was used as a meeting point during the occupation. Mdm. Lim describes how the association helped distribute rice and other goods. She also mentions that the Japanese authorities required all residents to register at the association building. This is a useful detail for the chapter.

Interview 68-D (Mdm. Neo Ah Choo) – The summary describes the community kitchen that was set up in the shophouse district. Mdm. Neo recalls that the kitchen was run by a group of women from the neighbourhood. They cooked porridge and distributed it to the elderly and the sick. She also mentions that the kitchen was closed after a few months because of shortages.

4. DATA SHARING POLICIES

4.1 The parties recognise that genealogical data is often sensitive and may relate to living individuals. Accordingly, all data sharing under this MOU shall comply with the Personal Data Protection Act 2012 (Singapore) and any other applicable law.

4.2 The following categories of data may be shared freely as “open data”:

(a) Records dated more than 100 years before the date of sharing;
(b) Names and dates of birth/death of deceased individuals, where such information is already in the public domain;
(c) Published family histories and newsletters.

7. TERM AND RENEWAL

7.1 This MOU shall take effect on 1 January 2019 and shall remain in force for a period of three (3) years, expiring on 31 December 2021.

7.2 The parties may renew this MOU for successive periods of two (2) years each by mutual written agreement. A party wishing to renew shall give written notice to the other party not later than ninety (90) days before the expiry of the then-current term.

7.3 Renewal shall be confirmed by an exchange of letters signed by the authorised representatives of both parties. The renewed term shall be on the same terms and conditions as set out in this MOU unless the parties agree otherwise in writing.

7.4 Any renewal shall be recorded in the minutes of the next joint committee meeting and appended to this MOU as an addendum.

7.5 For the avoidance of doubt, the obligations under Sections 4.5 and 4.6 (data logs and destruction/return of data) shall survive the expiry or termination of this MOU.

8. AMENDMENT

8.1 This MOU may be amended only by a written instrument signed by the authorised representatives of both parties.

8.2 A party proposing an amendment shall circulate a draft of the proposed amendment to the other party at least thirty (30) days before the anticipated date of signing, unless the parties agree to a shorter period.

8.3 Any amendment shall be numbered sequentially and attached to this MOU as an annex. The annex shall form part of this MOU.

8.4 Minor administrative corrections, such as changes to contact details or the names of authorised representatives, may be made by an exchange of letters without a formal amendment, provided that the letters are signed by the authorised representatives of both parties and reference this MOU.

9. TERMINATION

9.1 Either party may terminate this MOU by giving the other party not less than six (6) months' written notice of termination.

9.2 The parties may terminate this MOU immediately by mutual written agreement.

9.3 Either party may terminate this MOU with immediate effect by written notice if the other party:

(a) commits a material breach of any provision of this MOU and fails to remedy that breach within thirty (30) days of receiving written notice specifying the breach; or

(b) is dissolved, wound up, or otherwise ceases to carry on its activities.

9.4 Upon termination, the parties shall:

(a) complete any joint activities that are already underway, unless the parties agree otherwise;

(b) return or destroy data received under this MOU in accordance with Section 4.6; and

(c) settle any outstanding financial obligations between them.

9.5 Termination shall not affect any rights or obligations that have accrued prior to the date of termination.

10. DISPUTE RESOLUTION

10.1 The parties shall use their best efforts to resolve any dispute arising out of or in connection with this MOU through friendly negotiation.

10.2 If the dispute is not resolved within sixty (60) days of the date on which it is first raised in writing, the parties shall refer the dispute to mediation at the Singapore Mediation Centre or such other mediation service as the parties may agree.
